idiom_name: DomainEvent interface + Bus.Publish with per-type subscriber lists
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, so events are plain structs satisfying a small interface (EventName() string and/or OccurredAt() time.Time) and the bus is an explicit, mutex-guarded map of subscriber lists; handlers are typed functions or a generic interface, and registration happens in a bootstrap function. The language does not remove any of the classic structure - interfaces only make the event type cheap - so the design work is the dispatch timing, the error policy and the concurrency of dispatch.
pitfalls: A mutex-guarded bus dispatches synchronously, so a slow handler blocks the request; a goroutine per event needs its own error collection or panics disappear.
A handler that mutates the shared event struct changes it for later subscribers; treat events as read-only and copy slices or maps out of the aggregate.

variants.name: Generic subscriber registration (Handler[T])
variants.idiom_name: Handler[T Event] + ListenOn[T] registration keyed by reflect.TypeOf
variants.implementation_notes: With Go generics the handler signature is typed to one event, so subscribers need neither type switch nor assertion: type Handler[T Event] interface { Handle(context.Context, T) error } plus a registration helper ListenOn[T Event](bus *Bus, h Handler[T]) that keys the subscriber list by the concrete event type. Generics require Go 1.18 or later. Choose it for libraries and larger services where the type safety at registration is worth the reflection it hides.
pitfalls: The assertion e.(T) inside the adapter is safe only because registration is keyed by the same type; registering a nil interface value panics at the first dispatch.
Generics do not remove the bus: reflect.TypeOf at registration costs a little and moves type errors to registration time, where they are easy to miss behind interface satisfaction.
